title: Clocha na nAinmneacha
subtitle: The Stones of Names — Maigh Eo, c. 480 AD

sessions.en: The first greeting, and who you are
sessions.hook: Dáire will ask where you come from. Have an answer ready — anywhere in the world counts.

beats.n: Salt wind, a field above the grey Atlantic. A man kneels at a long pillar of stone, cutting notches into its edge with a chisel of iron. Wood smoke, wet grass, the tap-tap-tap of careful work.
He looks up, unhurried, and raises a hand.

pages.title: The greeting is younger than the stone
paras: That greeting is *new* here. Christianity reached this coast within living memory, and it rewired how people say hello: **Dia dhuit** — “God to you.”
The custom is call-and-response, and the response *raises* the greeting:
You never just echo a greeting in Irish. You answer it, and add to it.
pairs: — Dia is Muire dhuit.  (God *and Mary* to you.)

pages.context: The carver waits, hand still raised.
pages.prompt: He said “Dia dhuit.” What do you say back?

opts.why: You raised the greeting — God and Mary to you. Exactly the custom.
Understandable — but Irish greetings escalate. The reply adds Mary: Dia is Muire dhuit.
That's “goodbye” — a little early, you only just met him.

pages.context: He nods, pleased — then says it once more, slower, and waits. He wants to hear it in your mouth.
pages.g: God and Mary to you — the reply that raises the greeting

beats.n: He sets down the chisel and puts a hand to his chest.

beats.g: I am Dáire — ‘is mise’ introduces who you are

beats.n: A pause. A nod at you.

pages.title: The two “to be”s — what school never explained
paras: Irish has **two** verbs where English has one “to be”, and they are not interchangeable.
**Is** — the copula — is for *identity*: who or what something *is*.
**Tá** is for *states and conditions*: how something is right now.
You are not “in a state of being Niamh” — you simply *are* Niamh. Identity takes **is**. Half the confusion of school Irish dissolves right here.
pairs: Is mise Dáire. — I am Dáire.
Tá mé fuar. — I am cold.

pages.prompt: How would Bríd say “I am Bríd”?

opts.why: Identity → the copula. Is mise Bríd.
Tá is for states — cold, tired, happy. Being Bríd isn't a passing condition; identity takes is.
Irish word order is strict here: Is mise Bríd.

pages.context: Practise the shape on someone else's name first.
pages.prompt: Build: “I am Áine.”
Your turn — introduce yourself.
pages.hint: Type the whole phrase: Is mise + your name.

beats.n: He repeats your name once, slowly, weighing it the way other people weigh coins — then glances at the pillar beside him, its edge already striped with strokes.
“Names are my trade,” he says. “I cut them so they outlive the breath that spoke them.”

beats.g: What's your name? — literally ‘what name is on you?’

beats.n: Notice the shape of that: in Irish, a name is *on* you, like a cloak. The language keeps a small distance between you and what you're called. More on that another day.

pages.prompt: Match the Irish to its meaning.

beats.n: The light is going. Dáire covers his tools with a hide and lifts a hand.
Tomorrow he'll want to know where you come from. Have an answer ready.

sessions.en: Where you're from — placenames are poems
sessions.hook: A family walks in from the east tomorrow, bringing Dáire a stone's worth of work — and you a lesson in what your surname is made of.

pages.intro: The path down to the strand passes yesterday's practice stone. Overnight the wind has been at the chalk marks — the softest strokes always go first.

items.en: hello — the first words he gave you

beats.n: The tide far out, oystercatchers crying over the flats. Dáire is already at the stone.

beats.g: Where are you from? — literally ‘who from are you?’ (Connacht; you'll also see Cárb as thú?)

beats.n: He answers his own question first, the way a courteous man does:

beats.g: I am from Mayo — Maigh Eo, ‘plain of the yew trees’

pages.title: Every placename is a tiny poem
paras: **Maigh Eo** — the plain of the yews. Dáire's county is named for trees that stood before anyone carved anything.
Nearly every Irish placename works like this — a small, worn poem hiding inside the English spelling:
And if your people left, the poems travelled: Dublin, Ohio. Derry, New Hampshire. You may have grown up inside an Irish placename without knowing it.
pairs: Baile Átha Cliath — town of the hurdle ford  (Dublin)
Béal Feirste — mouth of the sandbank ford  (Belfast)
Cill Dara — church of the oak  (Kildare)

parts.en: church — from Latin cella, a monk's cell
Saint Ala, who kept one here

pages.note: A town up the coast from Dáire's yard — and the town nearest the field where this chapter's real stone still stands. The English spelling kept the sound and dropped the story; the Irish kept both.

pages.prompt: You want to ask someone where they're from. Which is it?

opts.why: Literally “who from are you?” — the Connacht way to ask.
Close — but that asks who they are, not where they're from.
That's hello. A fine start, but it won't get you a county.

pages.prompt: Match the place to the poem inside it.
Build: “I am from Galway.”
Answer him — where are you from? Anywhere in the world counts.
pages.hint: Is as ___ mé — put your county, city or country in the middle.

beats.n: He nods at your answer as if adding it to a ledger, and spreads both hands wide:
People will still be saying it on this island fifteen centuries from now — to tourists, mostly, but they'll mean it.

pages.prompt: Quick return to yesterday — and one new word.

beats.n: As you leave, Dáire mentions that a family is walking in from the east tomorrow, bringing him work: a stone for a man who died in the spring.
“Come early,” he says. “You'll see what the stones are *for*.”

sessions.en: Son and daughter — your surname was carved first
sessions.hook: Tomorrow Dáire makes you listen before he lets you near the chisel — ears first, hands after. Bríd finds this very funny.

pages.intro: You come early — the family arrives today. On the way past the practice stone you see the wind has been busy again.

items.en: where are you from? — yesterday's question

pages.place: Clós an tsaoir — the carver's yard

beats.n: They arrive mid-morning: a widow in a dark cloak, her grown son beside her, walking like a man carrying something heavier than the satchel on his back. They have come to order a stone.
A girl of about twelve slips out from behind the workshop wall and stands at Dáire's elbow, openly studying you.

beats.g: This is Bríd, my daughter — iníon = daughter

beats.n: He nods at the visiting young man. “And that is Colmán's [mac](turas://g/0) — his son. No [deartháir](turas://g/1), no [deirfiúr](turas://g/2) — the last of that house.”
Bríd is still looking at you — openly, the way children stare before manners set in. Dáire waits too. Introductions run both ways here, and the silence is yours to fill.

pages.cue: Either will serve — this is a courtesy, not a test.

replies.g: Hello, Bríd — greeting her by name

reaction.g: God and Mary to you — she raises your greeting, quick as a bird

reaction.n: She fires it back fast, delighted to be the one doing the raising for once. And notice what you said: *a Bhríd* — Irish puts a soft “a” before a name it calls, and the name bends under it. Bríd became *a Bhríd* in your mouth. More on that bending another day.

reaction.g: I know — everyone here knows everything

reaction.n: “I know,” she says — of course she does; she has been listening from behind the workshop wall for two days. But she nods, satisfied. You said it *properly*, and in this yard that counts.

pages.title: MAQI — your surname is an ogham formula
paras: On the oldest stones in Ireland, one word appears more than any other: **MAQI** — “of the son”. *X MAQI Y*: X, son of Y. That word is still alive — it became modern Irish **mac**, son.
Which means millions of people are carrying an ogham inscription around on their name:
Women's surnames answer differently: **Ní** (daughter of an Ó family), **Nic** (of a Mac family). Mary Kelly, in Irish, is **Máire Ní Cheallaigh**.
pairs: McCarthy — Mac Cárthaigh — son of Cárthach
O'Brien — Ó Briain — descendant of Brian
Kelly — Ó Ceallaigh — descendant of Ceallach

pages.prompt: The ogham word MAQI survives today as…

opts.why: Fifteen centuries from stone to surname. Mc and Mac names all carry it.
Ainm is “name” — but MAQI is the word for son, the one carved between names.
Fáilte is welcome. MAQI is the “son of” between two names on a stone.

pages.prompt: The family, matched.
How would “Mary Kelly” be written in Irish?

opts.why: Ní for a woman of an Ó family — daughter of the Kellys.
Mac marks a son. A woman takes Ní (for Ó names) or Nic (for Mac names).
Ó traditionally marks a male descendant — Mary takes Ní Cheallaigh.

beats.n: The widow speaks quietly with Dáire, and it is settled. The stone will say who the dead man was in the only way that matters here — by whose son he was:

beats.g: Colmán, son of Rónán — Rónáin is the ‘of Rónán’ form

pages.title: Why Rónán became Rónáin
paras: Look closely: Rónán → mac **Rónáin**. Irish names bend their endings to mean *of* — the genitive case. You don't need to master it today; you only need to *recognise* it: when a name shifts shape, it usually means “of”.

pages.context: Bríd chalks the guide-lines; you set the words.
pages.prompt: Set the inscription: “Colmán, son of Rónán.”

beats.n: The family leaves. Bríd runs her thumb along the blank edge of the pillar where the strokes will go, and looks up at her father, then at you.
“Tomorrow he'll make you *listen*,” she says, delighted. “He always makes them listen first.”

sessions.en: Learning to hear — the secret of Irish spelling
sessions.hook: Tomorrow you carve — for the widow, for Colmán son of Rónán. Everything this week was practice for that.

pages.intro: No chisel today, Bríd warned. But the practice stone still keeps your account, and the welcome Dáire spread before you has softened overnight.

items.en: a hundred thousand welcomes — his, when you told him your county

pages.place: An clós arís — the yard again

beats.n: He will not let you near the chisel. Instead he smooths a patch of dust with his palm and scratches letters into it with a stick.
“Before your hand cuts,” he says, “your ear must know what the marks are *for*. Stone doesn't forgive spelling.”

pages.title: The big secret: every consonant comes in two flavours
paras: Here is the thing that makes Irish look “unpronounceable” — and the moment it stops:
Every Irish consonant has **two sounds** — a **broad** one (leathan) and a **slender** one (caol). The vowels written around it are *signposts* telling you which:
Those “extra” vowels in Irish words aren't decoration and aren't all pronounced — they're **instructions**. Irish spelling isn't chaotic; it's a machine, and you now hold the manual.

pages.prompt: Which vowels are the broad signposts?

opts.why: Broad: a, o, u. Slender: e, i. That's the whole sorting rule.
Those are the slender pair. Broad is a, o, u.
Fadas mark length, not breadth — the broad set is a, o, u.

pages.prompt: In the name “Seán”, is the s broad or slender?

opts.txt: Slender — the e beside it says so; it sounds like “sh”
opts.why: Slender s = “sh”. That's why Seán is “Shawn” — the e was the instruction.

opts.txt: Broad — it's just an s sound
opts.why: The e beside it is a slender signpost: slender s sounds like “sh”. Seán = “Shawn”.

pages.title: An síneadh fada — the long mark
paras: The accent — **á é í ó ú** — is called the **síneadh fada**, “the long stretch”. It lengthens the vowel, and it is never optional, because it changes meaning:
Drop a fada and you may turn a man into grass, or an old thing into a person. The dead of Chapter 1 would want their names spelled right; so do the living.

pages.prompt: “Tá féar ann” — there is ___ there.

opts.why: féar = grass. fear (no fada) would be a man. The mark does real work.
That would be fear, no fada. féar — long é — is grass.

pages.context: Dáire turns his back so you can't watch his mouth — only listen.
pages.prompt: Éist — which word did he say?

opts.why: You heard the stretch — the é held long. That length is the fada doing its work.
Listen for the stretch: féar holds its vowel longer than fear does.

pages.prompt: In “cáil” (fame), is the c broad or slender?

opts.txt: Broad — á is a broad signpost
opts.why: a/o/u (with or without fada) mean broad. Broad c, like English “caw”.

opts.txt: Slender — the i makes it slender
opts.why: The signpost that matters is the one beside the consonant: c sits next to á. Broad.

pages.context: Dáire scratches a name in the dust: “Is mise Sean.” Something is missing.
pages.prompt: Carve the name as it should be.
pages.hint: Use the fada keys below the box.

pages.prompt: Which did he say?

opts.why: Both begin with the slender “sh” — the e is the signpost. The held á is what names the man.
Both start with “sh” here — the difference is the fada: Seán holds its á long.

beats.n: He wipes the dust smooth and says the old spelling law aloud, half chant, half proverb — the rule every Irish writer since has obeyed:

beats.s: Caol le caol agus leathan le leathan.
beats.g: Slender with slender and broad with broad — the vowels flanking a consonant must agree
beats.ph: kweel leh kweel AH-gus LAH-han leh LAH-han

beats.n: From now on, Irish words will look different to you — not tangles of letters, but signposted roads.
“Tomorrow,” he says, handing you the chisel to hold — just hold — “we carve.”

pages.intro: Carving day. You come down the path in the half-dark before dawn — and stop, the way you always do now, at the first stone. One last time before the real one.

items.en: the reply that raises the greeting — your very first phrase

pages.place: Breacadh an lae — dawn, no wind

beats.n: The pillar lies across two trestles, its edge chalked where the strokes will go. Bríd holds the line taut; Dáire holds the chisel out to you.
“Every stroke you earn,” he says, “you cut.”
Everything you've learned this week is in your hands now.

pages.prompt: You reply —

opts.why: Raised, not echoed. You've got it.
Raise it: Dia is Muire dhuit.
A lovely phrase — but it's the welcome you give at your own door, not the answer to hello.

pages.prompt: Welcome her — build: “A hundred thousand welcomes.”

pages.context: Dáire quizzes you as you work.
pages.prompt: Match the Irish to its meaning.

pages.context: Talk turns to the widow's people.
pages.prompt: Her maiden name was Ní Bhriain. That tells you she was —

opts.txt: a daughter of the Ó Briain family
opts.why: Ní marks a woman of an Ó family — descendant of Brian.

opts.txt: a son of the Ó Briain family
opts.why: Sons carry Ó (or Mac). Ní is the daughter's form.
It's family, not geography — daughter of the descendants of Brian.

pages.context: Bríd chalks the farewell of the dead onto the trestle, but her fadas are missing: “Slan go foill.”
pages.prompt: Carve it correctly.

beats.n: By late afternoon it is done. You cut four of the strokes yourself — Dáire guided the chisel but not the choice. The pillar stands; the family stands before it; nobody speaks for a long time.
Along the edge, reading from the bottom up, the way ogham is always read:

pages.caption: COLMÁN MAC RÓNÁIN — read upward from the base, strokes cut along the stone's edge

pages.ga: Is buaine focal ná toice an tsaoil.
pages.en: A word is more enduring than the world's wealth.
pages.note: Your first seanfhocal — proverb. Dáire's whole trade, in eight words. Collected to your museum.

beats.n: A stone very like the one you helped carve is still standing in a field near Killala — the Breastagh ogham stone, leaning into the same salt wind. The farm around it has changed hands a hundred times. The strokes are still legible.
The wealth went. The words stayed. That is the whole story of this app, and you've just lived its first chapter.

paras: **Caibidil a Dó — Oileán na Naomh** is next: a monastery scriptorium at dawn, a race to finish a great gospel book before winter, and a small white cat named Pangur Bán who will teach you the present tense.
You're testing a prototype — after finishing, please tell us: what pulled you back, and what didn't? That answer shapes everything we build next.

visits.frame: He greeted you first — Dia dhuit! — and the wind is still waiting for your half of it.
“Cé thusa?” — he's testing whether the wind took your name.
She wants to know where you're from — Cé as thú? Answer with your own county.
A family is walking in from the east. Someone must welcome them — all hundred thousand of them.
The widow asks how her son's name will read on the stone. Say it as it will be carved.
The evening light catches the carver's rule, half-silted with dust. Cut it fresh before dark.
